name: Borong
confidence_why: Two first-hand descriptions by the same author, both checked against held copies (Olkkonen 2000 phonology ms, SIL L&CA 43564; Olkkonen 2001 OPD); the 2000 ms is the fuller statement and adds secondary stress. 3 other works consulted do not describe Borong stress: Olkkonen & Olkkonen 2000 grammar ms (SIL L&CA 43532; 0 hits for stress/accent in the text we hold); McElhanon 1973 (held text, 0 hits for stress/accent); Suter 2018 (comparative morphology; its one Borong-related stress remark is that a reconstructed suffix *-utup 'carried no primary stress' in Borong, Somba, Kinalaknga and Kumukio, a diachronic aside, not a statement of Borong stress placement).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls on the first syllable of the word. Vowel length is phonemic (five short vs. five long vowels) and is treated separately from stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement in a one-sentence suprasegmentals note of a 6-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet; no examples with stress marked, no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of long-vowel interaction with stress. The OPD sheet is the standardized summary of Olkkonen's 2000 'Borong (Kosorong) phonology' manuscript (cited in its bibliography), which was not located.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD's title, language code [KSR], location (between Mindik and Pindiu, Morobe), villages (Ebebang, Hamoronong) and the recorded text are Borong/Kosorong = boro1279; but its running page header on pp. 2-6 reads 'Burum-Mindik [Mindik dialect] (Somba-Siawari) OPD', a template artifact from the Olkkonens' primary language Somba-Siawari (Burum-Mindik), and the PDF metadata title is 'Borong-Kosorong_ksr.rtf'. Dialect not specified (Ethnologue/IEL list Kosorong and Yangeborong dialects); the data appear to be from the Kosorong (Ebebang) area. Glottolog's 6-page 'Borong organised phonology data' (Olkkonen 2001, ref 20563) matches this sheet ('Data checked by: Soini Olkkonen (2001)').

new_statements.quote: 5. SUPRASEGMENTALS The suprasegmental elements: The stress is always on the first syllable of the word. A secondary stress occurs on the third (and fifth) syllable. No contrastive tone (pitch) on word level, no nasality.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog record (fixed initial stress, from the 2001 OPD p. 4 'The stress is predictably on the first syllable'); the 2000 phonology manuscript, which is the primary description the OPD condenses, adds the secondary-stress pattern (third and fifth syllables) and the explicit statement that there is no contrastive word-level tone. No contradiction. The grammar ms (43532) is silent on stress; McElhanon 1973 and Suter 2018 (held, read earlier) remain silent for Borong.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fixed and non-contrastive: primary stress always falls on the first syllable of the word; secondary stresses fall on the third and, in long enough words, the fifth syllable (left-to-right alternating rhythm). There is no contrastive word-level tone and no contrastive nasality; vowel length is contrastive but is not said to affect stress placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Stated explicitly: 'A secondary stress occurs on the third (and fifth) syllable' - i.e. alternating secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables counting from the left after the initial primary.
new_statements.exceptions: None. The statement is categorical ('always on the first syllable'); no weight, length or morphological conditions and no exceptional words are given. The 2001 OPD restatement says 'predictably on the first syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Borong (Kosorong) [ksr], Eastern Huon family, South Central Huon Peninsula (Morobe Province, PNG), main villages Ebebaang and Hamoronong; Olkkonen 2000 describes the (Highland) Borong dialect, noting that the Lowland dialect Yangeborong (90% cognate) is nearly extinct, so 'practically there is only one dialect'. Not to be confused with the neighbouring Somba-Siawari (Burum-Mindik) [bmu], Western Huon, which the same authors also described and whose dictionaries appear in the ksr listing by cross-tagging.
